basics.name: Prioteasa Cristi Andrei
basics.label: M.Sc. Data and Computer Science student, University of Heidelberg
basics.summary: Master's student in data science with an extended background and interest in cognitive science, philosophy (of mind, of neuroscience) and psychopathology. Interested in how AI interaction and exposure to generated content shape belief formation and trust, including its potential for persuasion, manipulation and deception. Unique interdisciplinary perspective, sound technical background. Passion-driven and purpose-oriented. Lateral thinker. Interested in ethics (neuro and AI), social epistemology, the impact of human-machine interaction on identity, science communication and knowledge transfer (for education and regulation).

work.name: Max Planck Institute for Biological Cybernetics, Tübingen
work.summary: 6 months part-time research assistant position, followed by master's thesis (on-going). Cross-institutional cooperation between the MPI for Biological Cybernetics (Prof. Peter Dayan), the ML Human Behavior group of the University of Heidelberg (Prof. Georgia Koppe) and the Institute of Psychology, University of Würzburg (Prof. Andrea Reiter).
highlights: The project investigates mechanisms that underlie the formation, breakdown and repair of trust and how these are altered in young persons suffering from BPD during repeated social exchanges (Repeated Trust Games), using both model-free (mixed-effects modeling) and model-based approaches (I-POMDPs).
Investigating mechanisms of irritation and retaliation and how they inform decision making and planning.
Developing behavioral signatures of manipulation and deception, informed by theory of mind (level-k thinking) and neuroeconomics.
Investigating foraging versus comparative choice models of team decision-making under bounded rationality.
Learned more about social learning theory, game-theoretic paradigms, theory of mind and psychopathology.

work.name: Roche Diagnostics, Mannheim
work.summary: Full time 6 months internship in the Early Research Department, under Dr. Bhawana Thakur (academic break).
highlights: Responsible for researching and developing an interpretable ML methodology for predicting the concentration of a critical biomarker relevant to heart failure that integrated different channels of information, sampled at different frequencies and with different levels of reliability (e.g. demographics, real-time medical grade wearable time-series data, blood biomarkers, POC measurements).
Worked in an interdisciplinary environment, where modeling decisions had to be informed by expert domain knowledge from clinicians and communicated to non-technical stakeholders.
Adhered to sensitive data security standards and the EU AI Act, making model transparency and mechanistic interpretability a main priority.
Designed the model to meet a strict sensitivity requirement, where false negatives were unacceptable and false positives tolerable.
Improved my skills in hierarchical modeling, time series analysis and validation under limited data using expert priors.
My proposed framework was submitted internally for future patenting.

work.name: Machine Learning Human Behavior Group (Prof. Georgia Koppe), IWR, University of Heidelberg
work.summary: Worked on two distinct projects related to analyzing, modeling and forecasting time series data from repeated social interactions (~300 hours each).
highlights: One project, rooted in dynamical systems theory, involved extending the AL-RNN (under Dr. Brenner) to account for a linear control mechanism, openly available here (graded 1.0).

The other project investigated trust dynamics in repeated trust games using Hidden Markov Models: generated synthetic canonical trust profiles (cooperative, uncooperative, antagonistic, trust building) and tried to replicate the findings of King-Casas et al.
Investigated the effect of simulated identity and expression cues on trust building.
Fitted LSTM variants and explored learning optimizations (e.g. teacher forcing).

projects.name: Reward and feedback processing (Art of fMRI course, PD Dr. Martin Gerchen, Zentralinstitut für Seelische Gesundheit, Mannheim)
projects.summary: Task-based fMRI study comparing neural responses to monetary vs. verbal performance incentives.
highlights: Developed the experimental design for a reward-based reaction time fMRI experiment comparing monetary vs. verbal performance incentives; took part as participant in the scanning sessions, gaining first-hand experience of fMRI data acquisition.
Analyzed task-based fMRI data across two cohorts to compare neural responses to monetary vs. verbal incentives.

Organized raw DICOM data into BIDS format and ran a full SPM12 preprocessing pipeline: motion outlier detection, slice-timing correction, realignment, coregistration, MNI normalization, and spatial smoothing.
Specified first-level GLMs per subject with condition regressors plus motion, outlier, and physiological noise (cardiac/respiratory) nuisance regressors.
Ran second-level random-effects analyses, including one-sample t-tests per contrast and two-sample t-tests between incentive cohorts, with FWE and cluster-level multiple-comparison correction.

projects.name: The law of small numbers: how two digit events shape our perception of the world
projects.summary: An investigation into the unavoidability of biased decision making.
highlights: Wrote a conceptual essay on how decision making biases (e.g. over-generalization) are unavoidable given the limited experience of significant life events (e.g. an unsuccessful marriage, the upbringing of a child).

Argued that viewing belief updating through Bayesian updates is guaranteed to lead to biased outcomes in low data environments (as most important life events are) and emphasized the importance of social learning.

projects.name: Artistic Colorization with Adaptive Instance Normalization
projects.summary: Explored a joint method for the colorization of gray-scale images and color style transfer. We propose an architecture consisting of two parts: a style encoder based on a VGG19 and a UNet, tasked with colorization and enhanced by Adaptive Instance Normalization layers. Both the weights of the AdaIN layers and of the style encoder, on which they rely upon, are trained implicitly. Moreover, we explore the influence of the chosen colorization loss (MSE vs LPIPS), the chosen colorspace (RGB vs LAB) and conduct an ablation study on different configurations of the network. Finally we show examples of colorization and color transfer from some paintings.
